look_here_first: Crew field ID: look for SILVERY, usually narrow alternate leaves on an upright low perennial. Look closely at dense pale velvety leaf hairs, not just a purple flower. Star-shaped violet/blue (occasionally white) flowers have a yellow center with 5–6 closely clustered anthers; branches MAY have orange-tan prickles, but unarmed plants occur. Young round berries are pale green with DARK GREEN STRIPES; fully ripe berries turn YELLOW/ORANGE and lose the stripes. Stems can resprout from creeping underground roots/rhizomes. Do not eat any fruit.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Solanaceae/Solanum: alternate leaves, 5-parted rotate or star-shaped corollas, poricidal anthers, and berry fruits; prickles and stellate hairs occur in many species.
best_field_traits: rhizomatous clonal perennial, often in groups
dense pale/silvery stellate or scale-like leaf hair felt
alternate generally narrow lanceolate to wavy oblong leaves
golden/orange-brown straight prickles may occur but may also be ABSENT
yellow anthers near the center, often nearly equal but sometimes unequal; NOT long, isolated buffalobur-style arched anther
green young berries with dark GREEN vertical stripes
fully ripe exposed yellow/orange berries with stripes gone
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The SILVER LEAF FELT plus exposed two-stage berries is the strongest combination. Solanum dimidiatum (not 'C. dimidiatum') is broadly lobed/greener with often much larger fruits. S. rostratum (buffalobur) has YELLOW flowers, strikingly long curved anther, and fruit enclosed in giant prickly calyx. Anthers of silverleaf may be somewhat unequal, so reject the 'exactly equal' shortcut.
crew_20_second_sequence: 1 — RECOGNIZE: upright to ascending patch of very silvery-gray, fairly narrow or sometimes broader wavy-edged leaves. Leaf blades alternate, not opposite.
2 — LOOK CLOSER: the silver coating is made of very dense tiny fused-rayed star-shaped hairs (scale-like/stellate); individual hair stars need a strong hand lens, not a routine field photo.
3 — FLOWER: find a blue-violet, 5–6-lobed star with yellow center and several yellow anthers clustered around the style. The anthers can be somewhat unequal—do not assert they are exactly identical.
4 — CHECK PRICKLES: many plants have scattered sharp straight GOLDEN/ORANGE stem spines (prickles) but some populations/young shoots lack them. The absence of prickles does not rule out silverleaf.
5 — FRUIT: green BERRY with dark vertical stripes when developing; later glossy YELLOW/ORANGE nearly round berry, with a small residual calyx, not a spiny bur.
6 — RULE OUT LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES: green, BROAD/deeply lobed western horsenettle, or bright YELLOW-flowered heavily armed buffalobur with a spiny enclosing fruiting calyx.
morphology_keys.habit: Long-lived clonal perennial or small subshrub, commonly 30–70 cm and sometimes approaching 1 m. Produces creeping deep-rooted belowground runners/rhizomes and new ramets; nearby shoots may form colonies. Root anatomy is NOT visible in standard aboveground study photos.
morphology_keys.leaves: ALTERNATE (one per stem node), simple, usually lanceolate to narrowly oblong, sometimes broadly elliptic or lobed; margins often wavy. UT Williamson County treatment measures leaf blades approximately 35–125 × 10–57 mm. Both surfaces may appear pale gray/silver, commonly the underside more densely so. Blade width, wavy margins and silver intensity vary.
morphology_keys.hairs: The gray sheen is densely overlapping stellate/lepidote trichomes, with rays fused near center. A visible silvery FELT indicates these hairs, but do not label individual microscopically tiny hair arms without a genuine magnified specimen photo. The surface can appear silver-white even where the precise hair shape is unresolved.
morphology_keys.prickles: Often straight, sharp needlelike golden- or orange-brown stem emergences; Williamson County treatment reports ~1.5–5 mm. Prickles may also occur on pedicels, calyces and leaf veins. They are NOT branched thorns; plants may be entirely unarmed, so their presence is supporting rather than obligatory.
morphology_keys.flowers: Typically 5, sometimes 6, blue-purple or violet corolla lobes, often roughly 20–40 mm across with a yellow starry throat; white-flowered variants occur. Five or six bright yellow elongated anthers are clustered near the center, sometimes differing modestly in length. The flower may expose an exserted style with stigma; anther terminal pores require magnification and cannot be positively pinpointed in the existing ordinary flower photo.
morphology_keys.fruit_stages: Immature berries ~8–15 mm, light/grayish green with prominent darker GREEN LONGITUDINAL STRIPES (not a miniature watermelon species). On maturation the stripes disappear and the berries turn YELLOW to orange-brown. The small green-to-dry calyx persists around the stem attachment, not expanded into a spiny bur like S. rostratum.
morphology_keys.central_texas_context: Dry rangeland, disturbed prairie/openings, roadsides, field edges and perennial beds in Hays/Williamson-area conditions. Species may resprout from underground root material after mowing or disturbance. A crew should identify before deciding whether a colony is intended/acceptable in the site.
morphology_keys.crew_management_and_safety: All parts, especially leaves and fruits, contain toxic glycoalkaloid compounds; do not taste berries and caution around livestock, pets, or children. Texas A&M describes it as poisonous to livestock and difficult to control where it spreads from roots. Distinguish ecological value from site management: keep a record of patches, seed set, and soil disturbance; do not automatically treat all native-looking wildflowers as beneficial in a managed bed.

botanical_terms.Stellate trichome: Tiny star-shaped hair. Numerous overlapping pale hairs make the leaves feel/look silvery; individual stars need magnification.
botanical_terms.Prickle: A sharp projecting growth from surface tissue, not a woody branch or true thorn.
botanical_terms.Anther: Yellow pollen-bearing part of each stamen, clustered near the middle of the flower.
botanical_terms.Calyx: Green outer cup of sepals below a flower or under a berry; NOT the berry itself.
botanical_terms.Rhizomatous / clonal: New aboveground shoots can arise from connected underground growing parts.
botanical_terms.Berry: Fleshy many-seeded fruit; a silvery nightshade's striped young berry changes color as it matures.

comparisons.key_distinctions: S. elaeagnifolium has densely silvery narrow-to-wavy alternate leaves and immature green-striped, then exposed yellow mature berries. S. dimidiatum has generally broader greenish deeply lobed leaves and bigger fruits, yet can also bear purple flowers. S. rostratum has conspicuous yellow flowers with a dramatically longer curved anther and fruit enclosed by VERY PRICKLY enlarged calyx. S. americanum lacks orange prickles/silver felt and has smaller white flowers with dark mature berries. Woolly croton (Croton capitatus) can superficially look silver-woolly but bears inconspicuous non-Solanum flowers and 3-parted dry capsules, not big purple Solanum flowers/berries.

field_matrix.leaf: Usually narrow or wavy, strongly SILVER/ASHY from tight star hairs
field_matrix.flower: Blue-violet star with clustered yellow anthers, sometimes white
field_matrix.fruit: GREEN berries with DARK stripes when immature → exposed YELLOW/ORANGE berries
field_matrix.crew_decision: Check silvery felt first, then stages of the round exposed berry.

field_matrix.leaf: Larger GREEN to green-gray, broad and often deeply lobed, frequently with spines along veins
field_matrix.flower: Large bluish-purple star with yellow anthers; overlaps silverleaf
field_matrix.stems: Usually greenish spaced prickles; whole plant more robust
field_matrix.fruit: Usually larger ~25–30 mm, young striped green, mature yellow
field_matrix.crew_decision: Western horsenettle can have GREEN-STRIPED young berries and exposed YELLOW RIPE berries TOO. Look for larger roughly 25–30 mm ripe fruits and broad green lobed foliage; color alone is useless. Photo comparison is not same-scale.

field_matrix.leaf: Deep irregular lobes; greener, armed and coarse
field_matrix.flower: Bright YELLOW flower with ONE strikingly long curved brownish/yellow anther
field_matrix.fruit: Berry hidden INSIDE enlarged SPINY enclosing calyx; not an exposed smooth yellow fruit
field_matrix.crew_decision: Yellow flower + conspicuously uneven anther + SPINY bur-like calyx.

field_matrix.leaf: Green ovate leaves and unarmed shoots
field_matrix.flower: Much smaller usually WHITE star flowers
field_matrix.fruit: Glossy dark/black ripe berries, calyx usually reflexed backward
field_matrix.crew_decision: Small white flowers and black ripe berries; not the silvery felt and exposed yellow fruit.

field_matrix.leaf: Woolly/hairy silvery-ish herb, generally greener and different venation/leaf habit
field_matrix.flower: Small inconspicuous separate male/female Croton flowers, NO yellow-anthered purple Solanum star
field_matrix.fruit: Three-segmented dry capsule, not a round berry
field_matrix.crew_decision: If not flowering, wait for reproductive evidence rather than assuming every woolly leaf is Solanum.

do_not_trust_alone: Purple flower alone: both silverleaf and western horsenettle may have similar star-shaped purple flowers.
Spines alone: silverleaf may be unarmed, and several other Solanum are prickly.
Berry color alone: both silverleaf and western horsenettle can turn yellow; compare SIZE, hairy leaf shape and fruiting calyx.
Apparent individual star hairs in an ordinary photograph: those hairs need a genuine hand lens / microscope macro.
Calling the five yellow anthers precisely EQUAL: silverleaf can be somewhat heterantherous, whereas buffalobur is markedly asymmetrical.
Assuming a single shoot came from seed rather than a rhizome: belowground connections cannot be diagnosed from habit photos.

visual_comparison.title: Silverleaf nightshade — follow the silver leaves, yellow flower center and two berry stages
visual_comparison.subtitle: Eight study panels: five exact-species photos (all with anatomy arrows) plus THREE distinct CC-safe look-alike views: western horsenettle ripe yellow berries and buffalobur's yellow flower and spiny calyx.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: SILVERY alternate leaves + purple star with clustered yellow anthers + exposed green-striped → yellow berries. Prickles support the ID but might be absent.

items.label: 1 — Whole growth form and silver leaves
items.image_role: Upright, spreading colony-like shoot with silver alternate narrow wavy leaves
items.caption: From a few steps away notice the silvery/ashy foliage and many narrow, somewhat wavy-edged leaves on branching shoots in open dry ground. This photo does NOT show the underground roots and doesn't resolve individual stellate hairs.
items.why_it_matters: Waxy green or deeply cut leaves are less typical; whole habit should be used with close leaves, flowers and fruit.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: EXISTING_INSTALLED_IMAGE visually inspected 2026-10-20; no roots or microhair arrows inferred

items.label: 2 — Flower: five lobes, bright yellow anthers and pale silvery leaves
items.image_role: Two violet star-shaped corollas, yellow anthers, style and silvery narrow surrounding foliage
items.caption: The purple star is the fused petal COROLLA. In the foreground flower, distinct long YELLOW pollen-bearing ANTHERS surround a long whitish STYLE tipped by a small green stigma. The fuzzy silvery leaves are behind them; anther pores are too small to verify here.
items.why_it_matters: Purple Solanum flowers occur in other nightshades too; combine with silver leaves and berry stages rather than color alone. Buffalobur instead has yellow flowers and one strikingly longer curved anther.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: EXISTING_INSTALLED_PIXEL_INSPECTED; arrow coordinates target visible pollen organs, the stamens vs style, plus violet corolla; no anther-pore claim; 2026-10-20 user iPhone screenshot verified: yellow-anther tip refined to true lower-flower yellow center (42%,64.5%), style/stigma tip to visible projecting slender pale style on same lower flower (48.5%,56.5%); relocated style label to nearby right side to reduce crossing. Main global SVG giant arrowheads handled in site JS.

items.label: 3 — Young GREEN-striped berries
items.image_role: Several developing green round berries with dark vertical stripes and silver fuzzy stems
items.caption: The little green spheres with dark vertical STRIPES are immature berries of SILVERLEAF nightshade. The whole berry is exposed; the calyx remains a SMALL support collar. These dark stripes disappear as the fruit turns yellow-orange.
items.why_it_matters: Fruit stage matters. A watermelonlike green stripe is normal at this stage; neither species nor safety can be inferred by 'green fruit' alone.
items.creator: WDavis1911

items.label: 4 — Actual gold prickles on a gray felted stem
items.image_role: Macro photograph of golden straight prickles projecting from silvery felted stem
items.caption: This is an exact-species STEM MACRO: several pale orange/golden sharp PRICKLES project sideways from a very pale gray felted stem. These are not the tiny silvery stellate hairs, which would need more magnification. Some silverleaf nightshade individuals lack prickles.
items.why_it_matters: Shows what a prickle actually looks like rather than treating vague 'spiny nightshade' as a diagnostic rule. Supports, but does not prove, species.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: VERIFIED_RIGHTS_EXTERNAL; original 1536x2048 visually inspected 2026-10-20 from Commons; direct photograph shows golden prickles on gray shoot; original unmodified; source license CC BY 4.0

items.label: 5 — Mature berries YELLOW, stripes gone
items.image_role: Two ripe yellow smooth berries with long fruiting pedicels and persistent calyx collars
items.caption: These are RIPE, smooth, yellow berries, no longer green-striped. The brownish little collar at the top is the remaining CALYX from the original flower; berries are EXPOSED, not enclosed by a spiny bur. Nightshade fruit is not edible just because it resembles a little tomato.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the seasonal change; contrast buffalobur's fruit hidden in a large spiny enlarged calyx.
items.creator: Alex Abair
items.photo_status: VERIFIED_RIGHTS_EXTERNAL; source 1536x2048 photo visually inspected; CC BY 4.0; explicitly ripe Solanum elaeagnifolium fruits, photo pixels unmodified

items.label: 6 — LOOK-ALIKE: WESTERN HORSENETTLE also has exposed ripe yellow berries
items.image_role: Different Solanum species: multiple relatively large, smooth yellow mature berries on drying branched stems
items.caption: THIS IS WESTERN HORSENETTLE, S. DIMIDIATUM, not silverleaf nightshade. Mature berries are ALSO SMOOTH YELLOW, making color alone a TRAP. Williamson County botany documents western horsenettle often roughly 25–30 mm across in local material, versus silverleaf commonly around 8–15 mm; without a ruler this picture cannot prove the measurements. Use green broad/lobed leaves, berry size in hand, and whether the stem looks densely silver-felted.
items.why_it_matters: Genuine local look-alike photographed with ripe yellow fruits. Both species can also have green-striped juvenile fruits. If all you see is a yellow berry and a leafless stem, write 'Solanum sp.' until leaf/flower morphology and fruit size are checked.
items.creator: Vince Hale

items.label: 7 — LOOK-ALIKE: buffalobur's spiny enclosing calyx (NOT silverleaf)

items.caption: THIS IS BUFFALOBUR, a different species. The round 'spiny balls' are the enlarged PRICKLY FRUITING CALYCES surrounding hidden berries; the leaves are much greener and more deeply lobed than most silverleaf nightshade foliage.

visual_comparison.overlay_note: Yellow berries are NOT a species-level diagnosis: Western horsenettle (S. dimidiatum) also has exposed smooth yellow mature fruits, commonly substantially larger, but comparison photos have no matching scale. Examine mature fruit size, SILVERY vs GREEN/BROAD leaf blades, and juvenile fruit markings. Buffalobur hides fruit within a sharply spiny enlarged calyx. Neither look-alike is part of the main silverleaf gallery.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Silverleaf nightshade: silver foliage, yellow anthers, prickles and both berry stages
steps: Check silver felt on the narrow alternate leaves first (not a purple flower alone). Dense tiny stellate hairs create the gray surface; individual arms need magnification.
Flower: identify the violet/blue star, clustered YELLOW ANTHERS, and central STYLE. A spiny plant with YELLOW flowers and one huge bent anther is more likely buffalobur.
Look at both berry stages: unripe GREEN with darker stripes, finally exposed YELLOW/ORANGE; buffalobur fruits are hidden inside large spiny calyces.
Check prickles on the shoot for support. Silverleaf can be unarmed, so no prickles does NOT rule it out.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: All arrow labels indicate visible parts of actual source photos. Orange prickles may be absent on some individuals. The stars of single trichomes and anther terminal pores are NOT resolved in these field images.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: All Solanum fruit should be treated as unsafe unless independently identified and known safe; these yellow berries are not edible. Western horsenettle can also make striped immature berries and yellow mature berries—leaf width and fruit size are critical.
